strengths: The paper proposes a useful, straightforward combination of classifier-based Bayesian optimization with label propagation and label spreading. Supporting both generated unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools gives the approach practical scope.

The experiments compare both proposed variants against BORE/LFBO with multiple classifier families and GP-based baselines. Twenty repeated runs with standard errors provide meaningful empirical evidence, with particularly promising improvements on NATS-Bench.

The appendices investigate bandwidth, sampling distributions, unlabeled-data quantity, pool subsampling, and threshold selection. Including a no-unlabeled-data control and reporting computational sensitivity are valuable aspects of the evaluation.
weaknesses: The central explanation for improved exploration is insufficiently supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated locations does not ensure that high-density regions share the threshold label defined by the objective. Uniformly sampled synthetic pools likewise provide no demonstrated alignment between density clusters and objective labels. Appendix D explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. learning results do not apply directly to sequential BO, and does not establish the claimed beneficial expansion of decision regions. The illustrative acquisition plots alone cannot establish an improved exploration–exploitation balance.

The ablations leave the source of the gains unresolved. In Figure 12, the classifier without unlabeled data is competitive or superior in several settings, notably Bukin6 with label propagation and Branin with label spreading. This study fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta, and the corresponding control is absent from the application benchmarks. Comparisons against the supervised kernel estimator with matched bandwidth learning and acquisition-selection rules are needed to attribute the improvements to semi-supervised learning.

Several consequential experimental details are missing. These include input scaling, propagation stopping parameters, the label-spreading clamping factor, bandwidth-optimization initialization and bounds, and important baseline training settings. The description of 1,000-start L-BFGS-B also leaves unclear how candidates are selected from finite pools and how acquisition optimization is performed for the piecewise-constant tree baselines. These omissions limit both reproducibility and confidence in the comparisons.

The comparison with prior approaches to exploration is incomplete. Oliveira et al. (2022) is cited as addressing exploration in DRE-based BO, but its relationship to the proposed solution is not developed or evaluated. A compatible exploration-aware DRE baseline or a simple BORE/LFBO variant with explicit random exploration would directly test the paper's stated contribution.

Evidence for broader dimensional scalability is limited. All continuous benchmarks are two-dimensional. The 64D MNIST experiment uses representations trained with supervision on the same three-digit classification task; although the train/test separation is appropriate, this supplies favorable task-specific geometry and provides limited evidence for general high-dimensional black-box optimization.

A correctable mathematical inconsistency affects the algorithm description: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1}, while the text states P = D^{-1}W. This should be reconciled with the transpose in Equation (11). This issue is secondary to the unresolved empirical attribution and evaluation concerns.
